data.title: Starý Tekov – a hillfort and the seat of the Tekov county
data.excerpt: Starý Tekov is mentioned by the Hungarian chronicler Anonymus as the place where Borš is said to have founded a castle that later became the seat of the county, and by the foundation charter of the Hronský Beňadik abbey of 1075. The trachyte hill above the Hron, with a summit plateau 650 m long, probably carried a Slavic hillfort before the arrival of the Hungarians, but later building and above all the cemetery have destroyed most of the evidence.

data.metaDescription: A hillfort on a trachyte hill above the Hron, mentioned by the chronicler Anonymus and by a charter of 1075; later it became the seat of the Tekov county.

keyFacts.label: Stone feudal castle
keyFacts.value: Stood on the eastern part of Várheď, today completely gone; the defences went in stages from a palisade to a drystone wall

keyFacts.label: Várheď today
keyFacts.value: Since the end of the 18th century it has served as a cemetery, which has made more continuous archaeological excavation impossible

keyFacts.label: Romanesque/Gothic church
keyFacts.value: Remains of Romanesque masonry of carefully dressed tuff ashlars; the present Gothic church was built in the 14th century and rebuilt at the end of the 17th century

keyFacts.label: Monastic church (south-west)
keyFacts.value: Foundations of a rectangular building 4.3 × 5.5 m, polygonally closed presbytery, 16 graves investigated with no accompanying finds

keyFacts.label: Parallels
keyFacts.value: Like Bratislava, Nitra and Zemplín — the comitatus castles arose on the sites of earlier fortified Slavic centres

children.text: The village of Starý Tekov is mentioned as early as by the Hungarian chronicler Anonymus as the place where Borš, one of the leaders of Árpád's army, is said to have founded a castle which later became the seat of the county; it is also recorded by the foundation charter of the Hronský Beňadik abbey of 1075. It extends over a trachyte hill, originally encircled by two arms of the Hron. The summit plateau of the hill, rising in places as much as 10 m above the surrounding terrain, has the shape of an irregular ellipse (650 × 100–135 m), whose longer axis runs from north-east to south-west. By two cuttings of the road passing across the elevation the plateau is divided into three parts: the north-eastern, the central and the south-western; each of them had its own separate development in the Middle Ages. Trial excavations were carried out on all three in 1949 and 1968, and they brought some important insights into their occupation.

The most prominent is the north-eastern part of the hill. In plan it is an oval (c. 180 × 135 m), whose eastern, higher-lying part (measuring 135 × 70 m) is still called Várheď (Castle Hill) today; since the end of the 18th century it has served as a cemetery. The western, somewhat smaller part (135 × 110 m) has its summit plateau 3 m lower than the eastern one and is today built up with houses and occupied by gardens. On the eastern, higher-lying part of the hill there stood a stone feudal castle in the Middle Ages, of which, however, nothing has survived in the terrain. At the beginning of this century it was still possible to see at the site the remains of earthen defences, that is of ramparts, which most probably encircled the elevation around its perimeter. But nothing has survived of these either, because the edges of the hill have been shifted considerably inwards into the former fortified enclosure by the extension of the yards of the houses below it (Hradná street), and so its area today is somewhat smaller than the original one. The excavations of A. Habovštiak and P. Bednár brought insights into the way in which the castle was fortified: in the first phase this was probably a palisade, which was later replaced by a drystone wall, and from the results of these excavations we may assume that the castle was not rebuilt in stone.

The excavation of 1968 produced, among other things, a fairly large amount of Slavic pottery datable to the 9th–10th centuries and in isolated cases also to the 7th–8th centuries. Because the whole area of Várheď has been used as a cemetery since the end of the 18th century, no larger undisturbed area has remained on it which would make it possible to trace the remains of the former features of the Slavic period from which these finds come, or the remains of the walls of the medieval castle (in the trenches only larger or smaller clusters of stones were encountered).

From the finds it may be concluded that the site was occupied already before the castle was founded by the commander Borš, that is, before the arrival of the Hungarians in this territory. Judging by the overall area, the character of the site, the configuration of the terrain and the remains of the earthen ramparts, it may be assumed that the settlement was fortified, or rather that it was a hillfort which could have held a central position within the whole of the lower Hron region and later of the Tekov county. A Slavic hillfort at Starý Tekov is also indicated by the fact that other medieval comitatus castles too arose on the sites of earlier fortified Slavic centres (Bratislava, Nitra, Zemplín). The site, however, was severely disturbed by the later building development and especially by the cemetery, and so the finds and observations mentioned will probably remain for ever only a torso of what could have attested its former importance.

The central (and most extensive) part of the hill is almost entirely built up with two rows of houses forming Tekovská street, which on the north-eastern side widens into a small triangular square with the church and the cemetery. The masonry of the present church contains, in part of the northern wall of the nave, remains of Romanesque masonry — a course of carefully dressed tuff ashlars on very solid foundations of poured masonry. Burials were taking place around the church at the latest already in the 11th century, as the finds from some of the graves (coins) testify. From this it may be concluded that the church too already stood here at the time when burial began, i.e. in the 11th century. Its form is hard to reconstruct today, because on its site the present Gothic church was built sometime in the 14th century and rebuilt at the end of the 17th century, which certainly partly made use of and partly covered over the remains of the older Romanesque church.

children.text: In the yards of some of the houses, medieval but also Slavic pottery datable to the 9th–10th centuries has been found several times during earthworks. From this it may be concluded that this part of the site too, which we may regard as the settlement below the hillfort on Várheď, was occupied already in the Great Moravian period.

The south-western (smallest and likewise built-up) part of the hill is interesting in that, according to tradition, a medieval monastery with a church is supposed to have stood here. The Hungarian historian P. Gerecze even states that the ruins of the church, whose presbytery was 6.05 m wide and polygonally closed, were still standing at the time of his inspection in 1895. That is probably why older people still call this locality Starý kostol (Old Church) today, although on the surface there are no longer any traces of a church. A short rescue excavation in 1968, on the site of one house that had been pulled down, identified part of the foundations of an older medieval building of rectangular plan with internal dimensions of 4.3 × 5.5 m, oriented with its longer axis west–east. On the southern slope of the elevation 16 graves of a cemetery were investigated, in which there were no accompanying finds, together with part of an ossuary. In the ruins of the demolished house more than 70 markedly dressed ashlars were found. All this suggests that a church really did stand in this place in the Middle Ages, and most probably a monastic one, as P. Gerecze also states. The rectangular building identified may be regarded as part of the monastery, while the overall plan of the monastery and the church could not be recorded more continuously because of the later building development and the limited extent of the excavation. It is surprising that not even in the written sources have any mentions of this site survived, despite the fact that these were buildings of the later Middle Ages.

During the Mongol invasion in 1241–1242 the castle did not provide sufficient refuge even for the burghers from the settlement below it. During their flight from the enemy the charter of privileges of Starý Tekov was damaged, and King Béla IV then transcribed and confirmed it for them in 1253. The castle is mentioned in 1206 and in 1240–1246, with the župans Geche and Verner named; the importance of the castle, however, began to decline in the second half of the 13th century, until in 1320 the župan Imrich de Beche transferred the seat of the county, and so the castle in nearby Levice became the new centre of the county.
